extracted.intended_audience: general readers and aspiring essayists/humorists interested in conversational prose and social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for composing witty, conversational essays and table-talk: how to use levity, slang, dandyism, and logical conceits effectively while avoiding common stylistic and moral pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frivolous punning
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning (quibbles or plays upon words) is an 'indignity to the human understanding' and tends to triviality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives examples of bad puns ('Why tertian and quartan fevers were like certain short-lived insects' — answer: they 'skip' a day or two; 'Why an onion is like a piano' — answer: 'Because it smell odious' quasi 'melodious') to show how punning reduces discourse to paltry equivocation. Use of puns can be amusing in moderation or set pieces, but casual punning at table-talk is condemned as frivolous and beneath reflective company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate in use of cant and 'flash' words
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual substitution of cant or flash terms for words that truly characterize their objects is a bad habit — such expressions become 'algebraic symbols' covering ideal nihility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cant/flash words add piquancy like a mushroom in a sauce but become 'toadstools' when they pervade conversation; they are 'blank checks of intellectual bankruptcy' that let speakers avoid precise thought. Do not proscribe such terms absolutely (they have a place), but use them sparingly and discriminately. Examples of overused flash words include reducing broad human experience to 'fast', 'slow', 'bore', or describing calamities as being 'a good deal cut up.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precise diction over vague catch-alls
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lazy, catch-all words (the author's examples: 'bore', 'slow', 'fast') that mask a speaker's inability to discriminate ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise language prevents intellectual laziness; a single participle like 'bored' should not be a substitute for trying to describe a previously undescribed sensation. Resist letting vocabulary 'deliquesce' into half a dozen expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use learned or foreign diction with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive or unskillful use of learned language (e.g., Latinized English) can alienate readers and distort plain speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: a tutor's English half turned into Latin, producing mock-Eclogues full of pedantic Latinate coinages. Writers educated in classics should avoid letting that habit render their English obscure or absurd; ensure that any learned turns serve clarity, not obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage a logical conceit carried consistently for comedic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A tightly worked logical premise, pursued consistently to its conclusion, produces a strong comic payoff (illustrated by 'The Deacon’s Masterpiece' / the one-hoss-shay which is built so uniformly that it 'ran a hundred years to a day' and then all at once fell to pieces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poem-model shows how making every part equally strong (removing 'weakest spot') yields the surprising, comic climax of instantaneous collapse. Using a single absurd premise and following its internal logic can create effective humor and surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn levity into crafted humorous forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Levity or playful banter can be converted into profitable, structured humorous pieces (e.g., rhymed problems, logical stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author does not proscribe philosophical speculation that approaches the ludicrous; instead, he recommends channeling such levity into crafted forms (he reads a rhymed problem by a friend the Professor). Use spontaneous wit as raw material for deliberate comic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making moral instruction solely negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the moral staple of your work consist only of negative virtues (abstinence) leads to emaciation of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral writing should not be only exhortations to abstain; it must also feed on 'the more nutritious diet of active sympathetic benevolence.' Balance admonition with positive examples and active benevolence to avoid didactic thinness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine aesthetic taste with courage ('pluck')
rubrics_metrics.description: Dandyism (fastidious attention to dress and taste) has worth in keeping standards, but without 'pluck' (courage, backbone) it is empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that genuine dandyism is allied with strength of character — superficial 'Sunday blood' or purely decorative fashion lacks the force of those historical figures who paired style with daring (Brummel, D’Orsay, Byron, Alcibiades). If cultivating style or refined effects in writing or persona, ensure they are underpinned by substance and moral/creative courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: In matters of intimate sentiment, prefer restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Better too few words from a loved one than too many; silence can be more effective than talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As advice on speech in romantic or delicate contexts: while a beloved is silent, 'Nature is working for her; while she talks, she is working for herself.' Apply restraint in expression where silence or minimal utterance has stronger emotional effect.
